messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi is an 18-year-old African American male police officer who sought help after experiencing significant distress related to witnessing domestic violence in his childhood. Kofi's symptoms have been impacting his ability to perform his duties and maintain a sense of safety. At the age of eight, Kofi witnessed his mother being violently attacked by her partner. The fear and trauma he felt that night were so intense that they have haunted him ever since. During the attack, he remembers feeling helpless as he tried to protect his mother but was unable to do anything to stop it. This experience has shaped his current beliefs about himself and the world. Kofi often feels uncomfortable in unfamiliar places because he cannot assess the danger accurately. The unusual silence in these environments heightens his sense of threat, making him hyper-aware of potential weapons or dangerous objects around him. These perceptions have led Kofi to avoid going to new locations altogether, which makes his job as a police officer particularly challenging. When Kofi is triggered by any discomfort or when people act suspiciously, memories of the violent event flood back. He experiences bodily reenactment, feeling like he is reliving the traumatic moment physically and emotionally. This triggers intense grief and overwhelming sadness each time these snapshots replay in his mind. The vividness of these memories compounds his fear, making it difficult for him to trust himself in dangerous situations. Kofi’s negative appraisals about his ability to rely on himself have further intensified his sense of helplessness. He fears that he is going crazy because of the intense reactions he experiences since witnessing the violence. This belief has reinforced his tendency to avoid triggers and unfamiliar places, creating a cycle where every perceived threat or unusual silence leads him to re-experience those traumatic memories. These negative appraisals also influence how Kofi perceives threats in his environment. The fear that bad things will happen makes him more vigilant and sensitive to potential dangers. This heightened vigilance exacerbates the triggers he experiences, leading to a cycle where each memory of the event reinforces his sense of threat and further undermines his confidence. Kofi’s current state is one of significant distress and isolation. He has become increasingly withdrawn from social interactions and even from his duties as a police officer due to his inability to trust himself in potentially dangerous situations. The fear that he might not be able to protect others or even himself is overwhelming, leading him to question whether he can continue in law enforcement. What finally brought Kofi to seek help was the realization that his performance at work had been severely impacted by these symptoms. He found it increasingly difficult to maintain focus and respond effectively during critical situations. His hope is to regain a sense of control over his life and his job, to no longer feel as though he is on the brink of losing himself entirely. Kofi’s most pressing fear is that he will continue to spiral further into helplessness and isolation. He is hoping for strategies and support that can help him manage his symptoms, rebuild his confidence, and return to a fulfilling life and career without being haunted by the past.
